41.quote_or_event: “Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows - O Nanak! Their faces are radiant in the Court of the Lord, and many are saved along with them!”
41.explanation: The closing salok of the Japji joins the two halves of the Sikh householder ideal, remembrance of the Name and honest labour, and says that such a life carries many others along with it.
41.tie_back: Like Valluvar's householder who is the steady support of those who depend on him, the one who works and remembers God is pictured as someone whom many others are carried by.
41.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib, closing Salok, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
41._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse affirms working householder life and its benefit to others, but the 'many saved' is spiritual rather than the material support of named dependants that Kural 41 describes.

42.quote_or_event: Sent by his father with money to start trading, the young Nanak met a band of holy men who had not eaten for days, gave them the money, and bought them food, saying he had spent it to the best advantage.
42.explanation: Macauliffe retells this Janamsakhi episode, remembered by Sikhs as the sacha sauda or true bargain: the first act of the future Guru's working life is to feed renunciants and the hungry from household money.
42.tie_back: It enacts the Kural's claim that the renunciant and the destitute eat because a householder provides, here literally with a householder's trading capital.
42.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter III, pp. 30-31
42._accuracy_note: Strong fit on feeding renunciants and the hungry, but it rests on the Janamsakhi tradition (hagiography), and it has nothing to match the Kural's third class, the dead.

43.quote_or_event: “He does not honor his ancestors while they are alive, but he holds feasts in their honor after they have died. Tell me, how can his poor ancestors receive what the crows and the dogs have eaten up?”
43.explanation: Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns the Gurus included in the scripture, mocks memorial feasts for the dead and offerings to gods made of clay, and asks people to honour their elders while they live and to remember the one Lord who has no ancestors.
43.tie_back: It speaks to two of the Kural's five claims, ancestors and gods, but turns them around: Sikh teaching keeps the duty to kin and guests and drops ritual offerings to the dead and the gods.
43.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 332, Raag Gauri Bairaagan, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
43._accuracy_note: Next-best only: this is a deliberate contrast, since the SGGS rejects the ancestor rites and offerings to deities that Kural 43 lists among the householder's foremost duties.

44.quote_or_event: At Saiyidpur Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo, a poor carpenter, and declined the feast of Malik Bhago, a steward grown rich by bribery and oppression. Holding Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Bhago's rich bread in the other, he squeezed them; milk came from Lalo's and blood from Bhago's.
44.explanation: Macauliffe tells this well-known Janamsakhi story to show the Sikh principle that food earned by honest labour is pure, while food gained by exploiting others is tainted, however lavishly it is shared.
44.tie_back: It is the Sikh image of Valluvar's two conditions: earning without blame and sharing what one eats; Bhago shares but fails the first test, and so his bread is refused.
44.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter IV, pp. 43-44
44._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on blameless earning and its moral weight, but it is Janamsakhi hagiography and says nothing of the Kural's promised reward, a lineage that never fails.

45.quote_or_event: “They are not said to be husband and wife, who merely sit together. They alone are called husband and wife, who have one light in two bodies.”
45.explanation: Guru Amar Das defines marriage not by living under one roof but by an inner unity of love and spirit, a verse often read at Sikh weddings.
45.tie_back: Like Valluvar, who says love and virtue are both the nature and the fruit of domestic life, the Guru places the whole meaning of the household in the shared inner life of the couple.
45.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee, Soohee ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 3, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
45._accuracy_note: Strong fit on love as the substance of the household, though it centres on the married pair rather than the whole household and does not name aram (virtue) alongside love.

46.quote_or_event: “O Nanak! Meeting the True Guru, one comes to know the Perfect Way. While laughing, playing, dressing and eating, he is liberated.”
46.explanation: Guru Arjan teaches that liberation is not reserved for those who leave the world; it is found in the middle of ordinary life, by one who follows the Guru's way.
46.tie_back: Valluvar asks what more anyone could gain by leaving a virtuous home for another path; the Guru answers that even liberation is reached within everyday life.
46.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri, Gujri ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 5, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
46._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the redundancy of renunciation for one living rightly in the world; the Sikh verse adds the Guru's grace as the condition where the Kural speaks only of virtue.

47.quote_or_event: “Yoga is not the patched coat, Yoga is not the walking stick. Yoga is not smearing the body with ashes... Remaining unblemished in the midst of the filth of the world - this is the way to attain Yoga.”
47.explanation: Answering yogis, Guru Nanak lists the outward marks of the ascetic striver one by one and rejects them all, placing true discipline in staying pure while living in the world.
47.tie_back: Like the Kural's householder who stands at the head of all who strive, the person who stays pure in worldly life is here given the very title the ascetics claimed.
47.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 730, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
47._accuracy_note: Strong fit on ranking life in the world above ascetic striving, though the hymn does not mention the householder or family by name.

48.quote_or_event: “How have you put off yogic garb and attired yourself in a household way.” … “You, while distancing and repudiating house hold life, go again to those householders for begging. Except their offerings you don’t get anything.”
48.explanation: Bhai Gurdas, the early Sikh scholar and scribe of the Adi Granth, describes the yogi Bhangar Nath at Achal Batala mocking Guru Nanak for living as a householder, and the Guru replying that renunciants who reject household life still live on householders' gifts.
48.tie_back: It is the Sikh form of Valluvar's boldest claim: the householder who keeps to virtue is stronger than the ascetics, who depend on him for their food.
48.source: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 40 (tr. Dr Jodh Singh)
48._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the polemic of householder against ascetic; note that the Vaaran are early exegesis, not scripture, and that this translation was verified on allaboutsikhs.com because searchgurbani.com would not load.

49.quote_or_event: “Says Nanak, one who meets the Perfect Guru, is celebrated as a householder as well as a renunciate.”
49.explanation: Guru Arjan does not set household life and renunciation against each other; one who lives by the Guru's teaching is both at once, a householder outwardly and inwardly detached.
49.tie_back: Valluvar calls domestic life virtue itself and grants that the other path is also good if blameless; the Guru keeps the renunciant's virtue but places it inside the householder.
49.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 496, Raag Gujri, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
49._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit, but Sikhism goes further than the Kural: it does not grant the ascetic road separate standing as a second valid path, it absorbs detachment into the householder's life.

50.quote_or_event: “In the midst of this world, do seva, and you shall be given a place of honor in the Court of the Lord.”
50.explanation: Guru Nanak tells his listeners that selfless service done within ordinary worldly life is what wins honour before God.
50.tie_back: Like the Kural's householder who lives on earth as one should and is counted among the gods in heaven, the one who serves within the world is given a place of honour in the divine court.
50.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 26, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
50._accuracy_note: Strong, close parallel in structure (right living in this world brings honour above); the Sikh version names seva and God's court where the Kural speaks of living well and the sky-dwelling gods.
